bio.en: Kenneth Berger was Slack's first product manager and is now an executive coach helping startup leaders make ambitious work sustainable without burning out.
bio.zh: 肯尼斯·伯杰（Kenneth Berger）是 Slack 的第一位产品经理，如今是一位高管教练，帮助初创公司领导者在不透支的前提下持续推进高难度目标。

summary.en: Kenneth centers his coaching on the idea of "ask for what you want," noting that voicing desires out loud dramatically increases the odds of getting them. He frames sustainable startup work as avoiding both burnout and sellout. The episode distills lessons from his decade as an operator and years as a coach into practical advice for ambitious leaders.
summary.zh: 肯尼斯把教练工作的核心放在"开口要你想要的"这一理念上，指出把愿望大声说出来会大幅提高实现的概率。他把可持续的创业工作定义为既不倦怠也不妥协。本期将他十余年运营者与多年教练的经验，提炼成对雄心勃勃的领导者的实用建议。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: You were famously the first PM at Slack and then you ended up transitioning into executive coaching.
turns.zh: 你曾是Slack的首任首席执行官，如今却转型成为高管教练。

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: For me, the impact was about making this work sustainable so that we're not burning out or selling out, but actually able to pursue these hard goals that we have in startups.
turns.zh: 对我而言，关键在于让这份事业可持续发展——既不透支精力，也不向现实妥协，而是能真正追逐初创企业那些高远的目标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What we're going to be talking about today is your personal magnum opus, the output of 10 plus years as a founder and operator and seven plus years as a coach.
turns.zh: 今天我们要探讨的，是你的个人力作——这份凝聚了你十余年创始人与运营者身份，以及七年教练经验的成果。

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: The core idea is ask for what you want. Turns out when you actually ask for what you want out loud, you're much more likely to get it.
turns.zh: 核心理念是：勇于提出你的诉求。实践证明，当你大声说出自己的需求时，成功的概率会大大提升。

turns.speaker: Speaker 3
turns.en: You're hired.
turns.zh: 你被录用了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How do you know that this is something you need to be working on?
turns.zh: 你如何确定这项工作值得你全力以赴？

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: If you're more in the people pleasing camp, maybe you're used to not asking at all. You're hoping that people are reading your mind. And if you're sort of more in the control freak camp, maybe you're used to ordering people around and saying, "Go do this now."
turns.zh: 如果你属于讨好型人格，或许你从不主动提要求，幻想别人能读懂你的心思。若你更偏向控制狂型性格，或许你习惯对他人发号施令，命令他们“立刻行动”。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: How do you know what you want?
turns.zh: 如何明确自己的真正诉求？

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: Complaints are great inspiration. Every complaint implies a dream. Let me envision a better future. Let me think about what's an effective way to actually move towards that. See what it's like to not be sort of living in fear all the time.
turns.zh: 抱怨往往能激发灵感。每一次不满都暗含着一个梦想。让我畅想更美好的未来，思考如何真正朝着目标前进。感受那种不再时刻活在恐惧中的感觉。

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: Yay. thanks for having me.
turns.zh: 太棒了。谢谢你邀请我。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that, yay. That should be a tradition that everyone goes with. I love that. So we originally met when I was doing a post on being a first product manager at a company. You were famously the first PM at Slack, and then you ended up transitioning into executive coaching, which is what you do now. What we're going to be talking about today is something that you described to me as, quote, your personal magnum opus, the output of 10 plus years as a founder and operator, and seven plus years as a coach to startup leaders. (00:04:59): And the core idea is simply asking for what you want, which sounds really simple. So let me just start broadly just why have you found that this skill, this one idea is so core to so many of the challenges that people run into in work and in life?
turns.zh: 我太喜欢这个主意了，太棒了。这应该成为每个人都遵循的传统。我太喜欢了。我们最初相识时，正值我为一家公司撰写关于首任产品经理的文章。你曾是Slack的首任产品经理，如今则转型为高管教练。今天我们要探讨的话题，是你向我描述的"个人巨著"——这份历经十余年创业者与操盘手、七年多创业领袖教练生涯的成果。（00:04:59）其核心理念就是坦然索取，这听起来很简单。让我先从大处着眼：为何你会发现这项技能、这个理念对人们在工作与生活中面临的诸多挑战如此关键？

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: If I had to answer in one word, it would be integrity. I think that it's one of these funny things where everyone thinks they already know how to ask for what they want. We all ask for what we want. We order our coffee in the morning and we all think we have integrity. No one walks around thinking, "I'm lying to myself all the time or lying to others certainly." And yet we tend to fool ourselves a little bit. When it comes to are we really pursuing the things that we want in life? And I think to me, the flip side of that is sort of the reason that the stakes around asking for what you want are so high because we can't guarantee we're going to get what we want. (00:05:59): But if we're asking for it regularly, if we're listening to the response, we're expecting the nose we get from the world, then we can get the sense of, "Yeah, I'm honoring what's important to me. I'm honoring the world's response and I'm moving forward towards what I want." And if we don't do that, "Well, then we're fooling ourselves that we're actually moving towards of what we want." There tends to be all these unexpected secondary and tertiary effects that come out of that of stress and frustration, and unhappiness because of course, asking for what we want, pursuing what's important to us in life is just one of the most important things of fulfillment, of what's important in achieving our purpose.
turns.zh: 若用一个词概括，那就是"诚信"。我认为这是一个有趣的现象——每个人都以为自己已经知道如何索取所需。我们每天都会点咖啡，都会觉得自己有诚信。没人会自欺欺人地认为"我在不断欺骗自己或他人"。但我们往往会自我欺骗。当我们审视自己是否真正在追寻人生渴望时，问题就浮出水面。而问题的反面则揭示了索取所需的巨大风险——我们无法保证一定能如愿以偿。（00:05:59）但若我们能定期索取，若能倾听世界的回应，若能坦然面对拒绝，我们就能获得这样的认知："是的，我在尊重对自己重要的事物。我在倾听世界的反馈，并朝着目标前进。若不这样做，我们就是在自欺欺人，以为自己在追寻所想。这种行为往往会引发压力、挫败感和不满情绪，因为索取所需、追寻人生重要之事，本质上是实现自我价值、达成人生目标的关键要素。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What are just some challenges that people have in their life and career that are just rooted in doing this badly? Not asking for what you want, not knowing what you want.
turns.zh: 人们在生活与职业生涯中因做得不好而面临哪些挑战？比如不索取所需，不清楚自己真正想要什么。

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: For me with clients, I think what I'm often looking for are just kind of this sense of being stuck because everybody has got frustrations. Everybody gets nervous at work sometimes. But if we're in the same stuck place week after week after week in our coaching sessions, probably you're trying the same thing and not getting any different results. It's that definition of insanity thing. (00:07:11): So really I look at that and say, "Okay. Maybe you're asking for what you want." Maybe. Although often people aren't. But even if you are, you're probably not achieving it. You're not getting the results that you want. So why are we not learning from that? Why are we not moving forward getting new data, trying something new, actually treating it as a sort of iterative development discovery process? (00:07:32): So I think that stuckness is one thing. And I think the other thing I look for is interpersonal conflict, right? Because I think that one mode of not asking for what you want well is holding back and not really saying it out loud. I think another really common mode is coming with a lot of entitlement of, "You know what? You better do what I say. I'm your boss. You're my report. You better obey or agree," or whatever it is. And of course the danger of that is interpersonal conflict. Even if you are their boss, that's a really disrespectful way to come into the conversation and it's an obvious source for a lot of issues.
turns.zh: 对我来说，与客户合作时，我经常会发现他们陷入某种停滞状态，因为每个人都会遇到挫折，工作中偶尔也会感到紧张。但如果我们在每次辅导会议中都陷入同样的困境，可能意味着你一直在尝试同一种方法，却始终没有取得不同效果。正如那句关于疯狂的定义所说："当你一遍又一遍地重复同样的做法，却期待不同的结果。"（00:07:11）所以我会审视这种情况，并想："好吧，也许你是在追求自己真正想要的东西。"但通常人们并非如此。即便你是这样做的，你也很可能无法实现目标。（00:07:32）所以我认为停滞不前是一个问题。而我寻找的另一个问题是人际冲突。正如我所认为的，不去表达自己需求的一种方式是退缩不言。我认为另一种常见方式是带着优越感，比如"你最好照我说的做，我是你的上司，你是我的下属，你最好服从或同意"之类的话。这种态度的危险之处在于会引发人际冲突。即使你是他们的上司，这种不尊重的沟通方式也会成为诸多问题的根源。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Before we get into how to learn to do this better and more of why this is so important, is there an example from your career where you did this really badly or you didn't ask what you want?
turns.zh: 在我们深入探讨如何更好地学习这些技能，以及为什么这如此重要之前，你能否举一个职业生涯中自己在这方面做得很糟糕的例子，或者你没有去争取自己想要的东西的例子？

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: There's so many examples. I think we will eventually get into the story of how I was fired from Slack. But I think for me, the thing that always came up was just being attached to being right. And I think a lot of us get into this boat. We enter into a meeting and we're sure from the first moment, "I'm right and they're wrong." And I think that especially in product management, we're supposed to be the holders of this vision for what the product should be. And so it's easy to come in with a lot of conviction and not really a lot of openness to other ideas. (00:08:51): Often what I try to introduce people to, and I've learned all this stuff the hard way, believe me, is it's fundamentally disrespectful to go into a meeting already deciding that you're right and the other person is wrong because you can't know that for sure. There's always a new perspective, new data that could come in. And so you want that conversation to really be a back and forth. And if you're coming in with this really ingrained sense of righteousness, you can't do that. There's no way to have that conversation.
turns.zh:
这样的例子太多了。我想我们最终会聊到我被Slack解雇的故事。但对我来说，经常遇到的问题就是执着于证明自己是对的。我们很多人都会陷入这种思维模式。参加会议时，我们从一开始就坚信"我是对的，对方是错的"。尤其是在产品管理领域，我们本应是产品愿景的守护者。因此，带着强烈的信念参与讨论，却对其他观点缺乏开放性，是很危险的。（00:08:51）  
我试图让人们意识到这一点——相信我，我也是吃了不少苦头才明白——在会议中就认定自己正确而对方错误，从根本上是不尊重他人的。因为你永远无法确定这一点。总会有新的视角和数据出现。所以你需要让对话成为真正的双向交流。如果你带着根深蒂固的优越感，就无法做到这一点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I think you may have already answered this question, but I think it's really important is how do you know that this is something you need to be working on? How do you know like, "I really need to pay attention to what Kenneth is about to tell me?" You said one is you feel you're stuck in your career, something you're just not making progress, and this could be the answer. Or you said there's interpersonal conflict and you're just having a lot of conflict with people. Are those the two answers? Are there more?
turns.zh: 我想你可能已经回答了这个问题，但我认为真正重要的是，你如何知道自己需要改进？你如何知道"我真的需要认真听肯尼斯要告诉我的话"？你提到一个原因是感到职业停滞，进展缓慢，这可能是答案。另一个原因是人际冲突，与他人频繁发生矛盾。这两个是答案吗？还有其他的吗？

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: I think those are great things to look for. I think it's also good to look for a sense of things being high stakes, because I think part of what can create a lot of conflict and difficulty in these situations is a sense of this is life or death. And that was certainly how it was when I was a founder of, "Okay, normally..." When I was at Adobe, it's a big company, they're going to be fine either way, no matter what I do. Right? I can be easy going. Let someone else have their way in the meeting. But when it was my company, when it was my vision on the line, I didn't feel especially flexible. The stakes seemed really, really high. (00:10:12): This is the success of my idea, of my vision, my reputation is on the line. And so I think often when the stakes feel high, we're kind of focused more on the fear of what we don't want to happen than on actually achieving what we do want. And that's a really critical distinction because if we're running away from our fears, it doesn't necessarily mean we're getting anywhere meaningful for what our desires are. And so that sense of high stakes that often we can get, whether it's in interpersonal conflict or being afraid of asking for what we want, that can get us really focused on the fears rather than focused on the goals.
turns.zh: 我觉得这些都是值得关注的要点。我认为，还要留意事物是否充满高风险感，因为我认为在这种情况下，引发诸多冲突和困难的部分原因在于人们会觉得事关生死存亡。以我自己作为创始人的经历为例，在Adobe这样的大公司里，无论我做什么，公司都能安然无恙，对吧？所以我可以比较随和，让别人在会议上随心所欲。但当涉及到自己的公司、自己的愿景时，我就不那么灵活了。风险感变得极其强烈——这关乎我的创意成功、个人声誉，甚至生死存亡。因此，当风险感强烈时，我们往往更专注于恐惧（害怕事情不按预期发展），而非专注于实现真正的目标。这是一个至关重要的区别，因为如果我们只是逃避恐惧，并不一定能达成真正想要的结果。无论是在人际冲突中，还是在勇于提出自己需求时，那种强烈的风险感都会让我们过度关注恐惧，而非专注于目标。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: There's a question I was going to save for later, but it's something that's very top of mind for me is knowing what you want. How do you know what you want? There's basically knowing what you want and then asking for what you want. I like equanimity in my life, and so I often don't ask for what I want or push down maybe what I want, or I don't think about what I want. I just want other people to be happy. (00:11:15): I'm curious what people can do and what I can do to get better at knowing here's what actually want, here's what would make me happy and fulfilled? What are some skills there I could work on and other people can work on?
turns.zh: 我原本想留到后面再讲，但现在最让我头疼的问题是如何明确自己的需求。如何知道自己真正想要什么？基本上就是先明确自己的需求，然后勇于提出自己的诉求。我希望生活能保持平和，所以我经常不主动争取想要的东西，甚至压抑自己的欲望，只想让别人开心。（00:11:15）我很好奇大家能做些什么，或者我自己能如何提升，做到更清晰地认识自己的真正需求，知道什么能带给我快乐和满足感？在这方面我有哪些可以提升的技能，或者其他人也可以努力的地方？

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: Well, first of all, I'd say you're very far from alone there. I mean, I think the people pleaser coping strategy is one of the sort of most classic, and it is effective, right? In the short term like, "Oh, you can feel safe and calm when other people are generally happy with you." And the cost tends to be long term in terms of am I really pursuing the things that are important to me? (00:11:48): So one of my favorite techniques here is this concept they call dream behind the complaint. Because you're right that we tend to not be that great always at really dreaming and envisioning and saying, "This is my dream of what I want out of life." That can sound really scary for people, but we're very good at complaining. Usually people are very good at saying, "Oh my God, there's this thing happening at work, it's so annoying. Or there's this person that really bothers me so much, why are they always like this?" (00:12:17): So the magic of that complaining is that every complaint implies a dream. It implies a better world where that complaint is resolved. And so often that's the tool that I'll take people to first to say, "All right, great. Let's complain. Right? It feels so fun and good and releasing to complain, and let's look at what that implied world is behind that complaint." What is this vision? And then to really check, "Okay. Let's imagine you get that. That's the world of the future that you get. How does that feel? Is that big enough or is it kind of meh?" (00:12:50): Are we like, "Oh, my dream is that I get to speak up a little more in meetings?" It's like, "Well, that's probably not a hundred percent of your dream. What's really behind that?" And so I think that check can help you sort of level up to say, "Is this really an inspiring dream for me that's going to motivate me more than those fears that might be hiding in the background?" (00:13:13): And on the flip side, with entitled people, you can also get really unrealistic dreams where I might say, "Okay. So it sounds like what I'm hearing is that your dream is that everyone obeys you and automatically agrees with you no matter what." And they sort of say, "Ah, I don't know if that's quite my dream." And so if your dream is so embarrassing to say out loud, you can't even really own it, maybe that's not the right dream. And so that checking whether it actually feels inspiring, but also sort of credible and possible is a good way to find that middle ground where, "Yeah, this dream is hard. I don't know that I'm going to get it, but, damn, it's worth trying. I want to go for it."
turns.zh:
嗯，首先，我想说你绝非个例。我觉得讨好型人格的应对策略算是最经典的之一，而且确实有效，对吧？短期来看，比如，“当别人普遍对你满意时，你会感到安心和平静。”但长期代价往往是——我是否真的在追求对自己重要的东西？（00:11:48）  
所以我最喜欢的技巧之一是所谓的“抱怨背后的梦想”。因为你说得对，我们往往不善于真正去梦想、去构想、去说：“这就是我对生活的渴望。” 这听起来对人们来说可能很吓人，但我们却很擅长抱怨。通常人们总爱说：“天哪，工作中出了这种事太烦人了。或者有个人总烦我，他为什么老是这样？” （00:12:17）  
这种抱怨的神奇之处在于，每个抱怨都暗含着一个梦想。它暗示着一个解决了抱怨问题的更美好的世界。所以我常先让人们去抱怨：“好吧，很棒。抱怨吧。抱怨的感觉既有趣又解压，让我们看看这个暗含的世界是什么。” 这个愿景是什么？然后再自问：“好吧，如果你真的实现了这个愿景，那未来的世界会是怎样的？感觉如何？这愿景够宏大吗？还是说感觉平淡无奇？” （00:12:50）  
比如，“哦，我梦想在会议上能多发言几句。” 但可能这还不是你梦想的全部。真正的原因是什么？所以我觉得这种自省能帮助你提升认知，问问自己：“这个梦想真的能激励我吗？还是说它被隐藏在恐惧的阴影下？” （00:13:13）  
另一方面，面对自视过高的人，你也会遇到不切实际的梦想。比如有人说：“听起来你的梦想是让所有人都服从你、无条件附和你。” 对方可能会说：“啊，我不确定这是否真是我的梦想。” 如果你的梦想太尴尬、难以启齿，或许它就不是正确的梦想。判断一个梦想是否能激励你，同时又是否切实可行，是找到中间立场的好方法：“是的，这个梦想很难。但该死的，值得一试。我要去争取。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that for someone that wants to try this on their own and help themselves get better at this without you being there, what is it that you do? Is it you dream about what would make you happiest? Is it complain and see what's at the root of it? Is it just imagine a world where you're really happy and see what emerges.
turns.zh: 对于那些想自己尝试、在没有你帮助的情况下提升自己的人，你会怎么做？是去梦想最能让你快乐的事吗？是去抱怨并探寻根源吗？还是去想象一个真正快乐的世界，看看会浮现出什么？

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: Specifically for articulating what you want because that's the first step of the asking for what you want process. It really is as simple as that of let's start with what you have consciously in terms of what you want. And if you have trouble, then we can try looking at complaints and starting to articulate a vision out of that. (00:14:29): But to me, really what's interesting about asking for what you want is that on the surface it's very simple, right? I mean, the steps I outline are articulate what you want, ask for what you want intentionally and accept the response and then try again. Because it's an iterative process. We're learning from the response and what it tells us because the response is usually no. So really what tends to be hard there, I mean, that's a straightforward process. It's not rocket science. What's hard there is the resistance. (00:14:58): The parts of us that are not so excited about that, that thinks asking for what we want is scary and articulating a big dream that we might not get is really scary. Because god, what if I don't get it? What does that mean about me? Am I a failure? Or what does it mean if I respect the no? What if I ask for my big dream and someone tells me I'm not going to get it? What does that mean? How am I going to feel? (00:15:19): So working through all that resistance is really a lot of what tends to be tricky about asking for what you want because otherwise it's articulate, ask, accept.
turns.zh: 具体来说，要清晰表达自己的需求，因为这是提出请求的第一步。其实道理很简单——让我们先从你清醒意识到自己想要什么开始。如果你遇到了困难，我们可以尝试审视自身的不满情绪，并从中提炼出一个愿景。（00:14:29）但对我而言，提出需求的关键在于表面上看它很简单，对吧？我的步骤很明确：清晰表达自己的需求，有意识地提出请求，接受对方的回应，然后再尝试一次。因为这是一个迭代的过程。我们要从对方的回应中汲取经验，因为回应往往是否定的。所以真正困难的部分不在于步骤本身——这又不是什么高深的学问。关键在于克服内心的抗拒。（00:14:58）我们内心总有不安的声音，觉得提出需求很可怕，觉得设想一个可能无法实现的远大梦想更令人恐惧。比如：天啊，如果我得不到怎么办？那说明我有多失败？如果对方说不行怎么办？我该怎么面对这种拒绝？（00:15:19）所以克服这些心理障碍，才是提出需求的难点所在。毕竟，步骤本身其实很简单：清晰表达需求、提出请求、接受回应、再尝试一次。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. You're getting into where we're going to go. Before we get there. Final question. This idea of dealing with, no, I think this is the other big blocker for people is like, "Oh, that's so scary to ask for something I really want or ask for something big that is really important to you." What is it that you advise there of just getting over this fear of just asking for what you want?
turns.zh: 好的，你已经说到关键点了。在深入之前，最后一个问题。很多人觉得，“啊，要去争取真正想要的东西，或者实现对自己很重要的远大梦想，太可怕了。”对此，你有什么建议能帮助人们克服这种恐惧，勇敢提出需求？

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: So I have a more expansive definition of no than most people, I think, because for me it's not a yes unless it's a hell yes. Because you really want enthusiastic consent. Not just, "Maybe, kinda. I'll try. We'll see. But yeah, absolutely, let's do this." And I think that often it's so tempting to settle for something less than that to say, "Oh, well, okay, we'll give that a try." And that often comes to bite us later on because we accept this thing that short of a hell yes. And then we realized later on, "Oh yeah, they weren't really in." (00:16:26): They didn't show up to the party or they didn't deliver on time because my CTO said, "Yeah, I think maybe we can deliver by May 1st." And then May 1st comes and surprise, surprise, your milestone is not done because you didn't go for that hell yes. And so I think part of what I encourage people to do is, one, to really hear anything short of a hell yes as a no. So it's not a bad thing. Mostly the world tells us it's actually really great data. It helps us figure out what are we going to try next? What are we going to try next, try next, try next? Because that's going to help us learn how to actually get to that hell yes. (00:17:03): And part of that asking process is of not settling for it, but actually asking and saying, "Hey, I'm hearing maybe you're lukewarm on May 1st as a date. What would be a hell yes day for you where you could say, absolutely, we can deliver on that?" And that way we're not making them wrong for saying no. We're saying, "Of course you get to say no. Everybody gets to say no whenever they want. But let's get to a hell yes. What would it take for us to get there?"
turns.zh: 我认为，比起大多数人，我对“不”的定义更宽泛。因为对我来说，除非是百分之百的肯定，否则就不是真正的同意。真正需要的是热情的许可——而不是那种模棱两可的回答，比如“也许吧，有点想试试看。先看看情况，但肯定没问题，我们就这么办吧。”我觉得人们常常为了图省事而接受这种不尽如人意的答案，之后却后悔莫及。比如，CTO说“嗯，或许我们能在5月1日交付”，结果5月1日到了，惊喜地发现里程碑任务还没完成。于是我建议大家，首先要把任何低于百分百肯定的回答都视为拒绝。这并不意味着糟糕——相反，世界通常把这种反馈视为宝贵的信息，能帮助我们规划下一步行动。比如，“他们对5月1日的交付日期没热情，那怎样才能让他们百分之百确定能按时交付呢？”这样既不会让对方觉得拒绝是错误的，又能引导他们给出肯定的答复。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a really helpful framework and phrase to use is just what would it take to get to hell yes? Not just what would it take to get to you feeling comfortable with this? What would it take for you to just agree to this? It's more a hell yes. And your point there is hell yes is when they actually fully agree. Oftentimes people kind of like, "Yeah, yeah, yeah, yeah." And then they don't actually follow through.
turns.zh: “那要怎样才能达成百分百的肯定呢？”这是一个非常有效的思考框架和表达方式。关键在于，怎样才能让对方百分百确定愿意做这件事？而不是仅仅让他们觉得“还行”或者“勉强同意”。要让他们真心说“绝对没问题，我们能按时交付！”

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: Some people call this a whole body yes because sometimes your head is saying yes, but your heart is saying no or your gut is saying no. And so I think you can really feel in your body when you've got a hell yes, when all of you is fully in and ready to do this.
turns.zh: 有些人称这种状态为“全身心投入的肯定”，因为有时你的头脑说“是”，但心却说“不”或“不确定”。所以我认为，当你全身心投入、准备好行动时，就能感受到那种百分百的肯定。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And this applies to, you're giving examples here of just getting like aligning a deadline. I imagine the same skill applies to everything in relationship questions and friends and family and work.
turns.zh: 这种方法适用于各种场景，比如协调截止日期。我相信同样的技巧也适用于人际关系、朋友家人以及工作场合。

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: It does. And it is something universal, but I do think of it as being particularly relevant to my work with startups because I work primarily with startup founders. Because with startups you know that mostly they fail. We all know the numbers on that. And so to me, there's a perspective you have to take if you're going to operate in the startup world of being okay with not knowing that you're going to get the outcome you want. A lot of people, we operate in a safer world where we're more clear exactly what the outcomes are going to be, but if you're a startup founder, you've got to be okay with, "I'm just going to go for this, and I know I probably won't get it. But it's so meaningful to me, I'm going to go for it anyway." (00:19:00): And so to me, that's not just about the big picture of running a startup, it's about really anything you might want in life, because that's such a useful perspective to say, "I know I'm not going to get it. I know I'm not guaranteed to get it. I'm not going to be attached to that. I know people aren't obligated to tell me yes, but I'm going to go forward anyway because I want it and that's enough."
turns.zh:
确实如此。这是一个普遍的道理，但我认为它与我为初创企业服务的工作尤为相关，因为我的客户主要是初创企业的创始人。要知道，初创企业大多以失败告终，这一数据众所周知。因此，在初创领域工作时，必须具备这样一种心态：坦然接受未必能达成预期目标的现实。相较于其他领域，我们身处一个更安全的环境，目标结果往往清晰明确。但作为初创企业创始人，你必须坦然接受：“我要全力以赴，即便可能失败。但这对我意义非凡，所以无论如何都要勇往直前。”（00:19:00）  
在我看来，这不仅适用于初创企业的运营，更适用于生活中任何你渴望达成的目标。这种思维方式极其实用：你深知成功并非必然，无法强求他人答应，但只要心之所向，便义无反顾地前行。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So let's actually get into the skill of learning how to actually ask for what you want more effectively. You already described three steps, so maybe just describe them again and let's just walk through them.
turns.zh: 接下来，我们来具体探讨如何更有效地提出自己的需求。你已经提到了三个步骤，或许可以再复述一遍，然后我们一起逐一解析。

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: The first step is articulating what you want. And we've gone into this a little bit, but to me, I think that the key places that people tend to have missteps here, or one in this phrase, it's fine. I think of the "it's fine" cartoon with the flames and the dog, I think it is. But I think a lot of us fall into that trap of saying, "You know what? I'm fine. I actually, I don't need anything. I'm good." (00:19:59): And again, this is tempting, right? Because it's so nice to have this idea that I'm fine, I don't need anything. And in a certain way, that's a nice attitude because yeah, we're not guaranteed anything, so it's nice to be okay with the status quo. But for those folks, often what I'm encouraging that do is to really tune into the parts of them that maybe aren't so fine like, "Gosh, I'd prefer it a little bit if things were this way or yeah, I'm a little bit bothered by this, or I'm a little bit nervous about this." (00:20:26): And so kind of tuning more into those subtle emotions that are pointing them towards, "Sure, I'm okay with the status quo, but I want something more." And so helping them articulate that in a clearer way where they can want something without being attached to having to get it. The other extreme of this is people who articulate these sort of wildly unrealistic goals. So this is the founder that just wants everyone to agree with him all the time and to obey him immediately. (00:20:56): So for those folks, it really tends to be more about saying it out loud. Once you say it out loud, it is clearer. That's not really what it's about. And so for those folks, I tend to ask them to go deeper to say, "Yeah, I know you're not a control freak. You don't want everyone to think exactly what you think. What's it really about? What does that get you?" And so often it goes from being this more kind of objective external goal to being a more kind of social emotional goal of, "You know what, I just want to have a team that feels really aligned around me and we're just ready to go for it and we've got each other's backs." (00:21:35): That doesn't mean we agree with each other all the time or that we're a hundred percent aligned in everything, but it doesn't mean there's a certain feeling that I have when I go into work. Even though I don't know that we're going to get what we want or that everyone is going to agree.
turns.zh: 首要步骤是清晰表达自己的需求。我们之前已经探讨过这一点，但在我看来，人们在这一环节常会出现误区。比如“没关系”这个短语，虽说没问题，但想到那幅狗狗被火焰烧伤的卡通图，我觉得这句话确实有问题。我们很多人都会陷入这种陷阱，说：“你知道吗？我没事的。我不需要任何东西，我挺好的。” （00:19:59）：这种想法确实很诱人，因为认为自己没事、无欲无求的感觉很棒。从某种角度看，这种态度也无可厚非，毕竟人生无常，顺其自然也未尝不可。但对于这些人，我更建议他们去倾听自己内心深处那些不那么平静的声音，比如“要是事情能这样就好了”、“我对此有点不安”、“我对此有点紧张”。（00:20:26）：这样能更敏锐地捕捉那些微妙的情绪，这些情绪其实在暗示：“是的，我能接受现状，但我渴望更多。” 接下来，要帮助他们更清晰地表达这种需求，让他们在渴望的同时不执着于必须得到它。另一个极端是那些设定不切实际目标的人，比如总想让所有人时刻服从自己的创始人。（00:20:56）：对于这类人，我通常会引导他们深入剖析：“我知道你不是控制狂，不想让所有人都和你想的一样。那么你的真正诉求是什么？这样做能给你带来什么？” 通常他们的目标会从客观的外部目标转变为更具社会情感性的目标，比如“我只想组建一支围绕我核心价值观团结一致、随时准备迎接挑战、相互支持的团队”。（00:21:35）：这并不意味着大家要时刻保持一致，也不意味着在所有事情上都达成百分百共识，但至少要营造一种入职时能感受到的归属感，即便我们不确定能否达成目标、能否让所有人都赞同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you have any examples from your time you could share of someone articulating what they want and figuring out how they articulate, how to articulate what they want just to make it even more real?
turns.zh: 你能否分享一些你身边的例子，说明人们如何清晰表达自己的需求，以及如何更有效地传达这些需求？

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: To me a lot of the classic examples are around feedback. Because I work with a lot of founders who are not the sort of classic control freaks. They're super nice and their teams love them and they love their teams. So for them, it can be really hard to deliver hard feedback, to deliver negative feedback and even more to actually create consequences. Because the thing about accepting other people's no is that, "Sure, they can always say no. Everybody gets to say no whenever they want, but there are consequences." And so the classic thing I see with the nice founders is they're really afraid to actually create consequences when people are not living up to their expectations. Right? (00:22:40): When they're not aligned with the culture, they're not delivering in the way that the CEO wants them to be delivering because it doesn't seem that nice. They're like, "Oh, I think of myself as nice and of being so kind and of people loving me." And it's like, "Well, that doesn't mean that there aren't consequences for their actions." (00:22:56): Part of really respecting them is respecting that they can make the choices they want and they're grownups enough that they can deal with the consequences of those choices."
turns.zh: 对我来说，很多经典案例都与反馈相关。因为我接触过很多创业者，他们并非典型的控制狂。他们人很好，团队成员也很爱戴他们，他们也爱团队成员。所以对他们来说，提供严厉反馈、传递负面评价，更是制定后果措施都变得异常困难。因为接受他人否定意味着：“当然，他们随时可以说不。每个人都可以随时拒绝，但总会有后果。”所以我发现那些友善的创业者，当团队成员未达预期时，往往不敢真正追究后果。是吧？（00:22:40）当团队成员与公司文化不符，或者未能按照CEO期望的方式执行任务时，他们往往会退缩。这些创业者会说：“哦，我自认为很友善、很善良，人们都喜欢我。”但现实是：“嗯，这并不意味着他们的行为不会产生后果。”（00:22:56）真正尊重他们的方式之一，就是尊重他们做自己想做选择的权利，同时承认他们已足够成熟，能够承担这些选择的后果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Can you even get more concrete there? Is it we need to hit this date, or are there going to be big problems? Or is it like, "I need you to hire this large of a team?" I don't know. What is it that they're not articulating that they later realize, "Oh, here's what I need to articulate."
turns.zh: 你能再具体点吗？是我们必须在某个日期前完成任务，还是会出现重大问题？或者是“我需要你组建一个规模这么大的团队”？我不知道。他们没说清楚的部分后来会意识到：“哦，原来我应该把这个说清楚。”

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: So I think sometimes it is about alignment, the disagree and commit. So I see that a lot of founders saying, "Hey, I'm super respectful of your differing opinion here, and I totally validate you and I appreciate you. Thank you so much for sharing that." But they're not willing to go that extra step and say, "Yeah, but this is the call and I need you to actually follow through with that. I understand that might be disappointing or frustrating or what have you, but part of the expectation for this role is that you can roll with disagree and commit sometimes when that's necessary."
turns.zh: 所以我认为有时候这关乎达成一致，即“不同意但承诺执行”。我看到很多创业者会说：“嘿，我非常尊重你的不同意见，我完全认可你，感谢你分享这些想法。”但他们不愿意更进一步地说：“是的，但这是最终决定，我需要你切实执行。我理解这可能令人失望或沮丧，但这个角色的期望之一就是，在必要时你能接受不同意见并承诺执行。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's an awesome example. I fully get that and I could see how scary that is to a lot of people. One is just coming to terms with, "This is what I actually want to be doing, but I just don't feel like I can because it's going to, I think, upset people." Okay. So what else can you suggest people do to help identify what it is they want and articulate what they want? So you talked about pay attention to just like, "Oh, this would be better. If this changed, I'd be happier." Or things would probably run better. That's a really cool example of how to think do that because easy, just like, "Oh yeah, if we actually can make a decision in this meeting, that'd be really cool." Maybe we should try to do that and ask for that. Is there any other tips and approaches to helping you figure out what you want?
turns.zh: 这真是个绝佳的例子。我完全理解这一点，也能理解这对很多人来说有多可怕。人们需要接受这样一个事实：“这才是我真正想做的，但我觉得自己做不到，因为我觉得这会让别人不高兴。” 好的。那么你还能建议人们怎么做，以帮助他们明确自己的需求并清晰表达自己的想法？你提到要关注那些细节，比如“哦，如果这个改进一下，事情会更顺利。”或者“如果这个改变了，我的工作会更愉快。” 这真是个很棒的例子，展示了如何思考和做到这一点。比如在会议上说：“哦，如果我们能在这次会议上做出决定，那就太好了。” 或许我们应该尝试这样做并提出这个要求。还有其他帮助人们明确自己需求的技巧或方法吗？

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: It always comes back to integrity. And a great way to do an integrity check is to just look have I fully expressed myself? And so I think we've talked a little bit about charting your feelings as a piece of that of like, "Yeah, am I really tuning into how annoyed I am or how frustrated I am or how nervous I am?" Because if I haven't fully owned those feelings and expressed those in whatever way is appropriate, then probably I'm not fully in integrity. (00:25:09): I think saying what you have to say is a piece of that too. "Gosh, is there something that I keep thinking about and I'm just like three or four days, I'm just like, man, I really want to say this to this person." At this point, you're probably out of integrity because there's something deep in you that really needs to say this, right? And so to me, articulating what you want is really about mindfulness is about checking for all these things. (00:25:35): What is the part of me that's not fully expressed? Because it doesn't mean I'm going to get what I want or that people are going to give me all my dreams immediately, but it feels so much better to have it out. That sort of suffering that fear usually comes from holding it in and saying, "Oh, having these stories of I'm not allowed to say that. It's not appropriate to express that I'm bored in this meeting." Versus saying, "Probably a lot of people would be grateful if we said out loud, 'I'm bored in this meeting.' Let's move things along."
turns.zh: 归根结底，关键在于诚信。进行诚信自检的一个好方法，就是问问自己：我是否已经充分表达了自己的真实想法？所以我觉得我们之前也谈到过如何审视自己的情绪，比如，“嗯，我是否真的在留意自己的烦躁、沮丧或紧张情绪？”因为如果我没有完全面对这些情绪，也没有用恰当的方式表达出来，那么很可能我就没有做到诚实守信。（00:25:09）：我认为说出自己的心声也是很重要的一点。比如，“天啊，有件事我一直念念不忘，过去三四天我都在想，真想把这话对那个人说。”这时候你很可能就失去了诚信，因为你内心深处有一种迫切想说出来的需求，对吧？所以对我来说，清晰表达自己的需求其实就是一种正念，就是去审视所有这些情绪。（00:25:35）：我内心还有哪些未被充分表达的部分？因为这并不意味着我能得到想要的东西，也不意味着人们会立刻满足我所有的梦想，但把这些情绪说出来会让人感觉好很多。那种恐惧和痛苦通常源于压抑自己的情绪，比如，“天啊，我不该说这些话。”“在会议上说‘我觉得这场会议很无聊’是不合适的。”而与之相比，“如果我们大声说‘我觉得这场会议很无聊’，可能很多人都会感激不尽。咱们继续推进吧。”

Vanta's market-leading trust management platform helps you continuously monitor compliance alongside reporting and tracking risks.
