I'm just scared to say this, to bring it up, to change the way people are operating to ask for what I want. What advice can you share for people to actually do this?
turns.zh:
本期节目由Vanta赞助。当谈到确保公司拥有一流的安全实践时，事情往往会变得复杂。现在，您可以通过单一平台Vanta评估风险、赢得客户信任，并自动化SOC2、ISO 27001、HIPAA等合规工作。Vanta的市场领先的信任管理平台帮助您持续监控合规情况，同时报告和跟踪风险。此外，您可以通过Vanta AI完成安全问卷调查，从而节省数小时时间。全球数千家公司使用Vanta来自动化证据收集、统一风险管理并简化安全审查。访问vanta.com/lenny即可获得Vanta 1000美元折扣。就是vanta.com/lenny。
（00:26:56）：好的。这也是一个很好的过渡。现在我有一种感觉。我需要改变这种状况。这种状况必须改变。我只是害怕说出来，提起这个问题，改变人们的运作方式，要求得到我想要的东西。您能给人们什么建议，让他们真正做到这一点？

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: So for asking what you want, I think the really important tweak here is asking intentionally because I think a lot of us are stuck on a certain track that's comfortable for us when we ask. And so if you're more in the people-pleasing camp, maybe you're used to not asking at all. You're hoping that people are reading your mind and just magically knowing what you want. (00:27:34): And if you're more in the control-free camp, maybe you're used to ordering people around and saying, "Go do this now." And so for both of those folks, it's not about... I think if you ask any of them, "Is this working for you?" They'd say no. Of course, it's obvious from an effectiveness standpoint, it's not working well, but they more just haven't embraced that you can do it a different way that they only really see one way of doing it. (00:28:00): So part of asking for what you want effectively is really just recognizing the rut that you get stuck in and working through all those narratives that make us resist asking it a different way. Because often the people who don't want to ask have a story that says, "This is too risky. Or it's not worth it. They're going to say no anyway, so why even bother?" (00:28:24): So these are all very common things that people go through, but then they end up not actually asking for what they want. Now, actually expressing who they are and what they stand for in the world. And that has a really serious cost. I think that we tend to tell ourselves the story, "Oh, this is fine. I'll be fine." Versus owning, "I'm going to be living my life not asking for what I want." Do I really want to be at my funeral and have people say, "Oh, Kenneth played it safe. He didn't really go for his dreams, but he was nice. No one was ever mad at him." That's not what we want people to say at our eulogies.
turns.zh: 关于如何提出自己的需求，我认为关键在于要有意识地去请求。因为我们很多人在提出请求时，总会陷入一种舒适的模式。如果你属于讨好型人格，可能习惯了不去主动表达需求，期待别人能读懂你的心思。（00:27:34）而如果你属于控制欲强型人格，可能习惯于发号施令，动不动就说“现在就去做”。对这两类人来说，问题不在于……如果你问他们“这样做有用吗？”他们都会说没用。从效率角度来看，这显然效果不佳，但他们更深层的问题在于不愿接受不同的表达方式，始终局限于一种固定的思维模式。（00:28:00）所以，有效提出需求的关键在于，认识到自己陷入的思维惯性，打破那些阻碍我们以不同方式表达需求的固有观念。比如那些不愿开口的人，总会给自己编织各种借口：“这太冒险了。不值得。他们反正会拒绝，我干嘛还要费心思？” （00:28:24）这些都是人们常遇到的困境，最终导致他们无法表达真实需求。真正的问题在于，我们不愿直面自己，习惯用“没关系，我会好起来的”来自我安慰，而不是坦然承认：“我要活出自我，不再委屈求全。” 当回首往事时，我们不想听到别人说：“肯尼斯太谨小慎微了，从不追逐梦想，但他人缘很好，从来没人生他的气。” 这绝不是我们希望听到的评价。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No. That's good motivation. Okay. So say in this example you gave of like, "I need us to make a decision. I know I'm trying to keep everyone happy, but we need to make a decision." Do you have advice for maybe phrases of how to approach. You talked about making intentional. How do you actually go about doing that? Is it the way you communicate it? Is it something else? How do you actually do this without pissing people off and also just risking too much?
turns.zh: 不，这很能激励人。好的。那以你举的例子来说，比如“我需要我们做个决定。我知道我想讨好每个人，但我们必须做出选择。” 你能给些建议，怎样用更有力的措辞表达吗？你提到要“有意识地提出需求”。具体该怎么做呢？是通过沟通方式？还是其他方法？怎样既不惹人反感，又能有效传达需求？

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: Even implicit in that question, to me that's that question of, "Oh, how do I do it without being any risk of ever pissing anyone off?" That's a piece of the resistance right there. And so this is a great example of the type of work that we have to do, right? Because in theory, asking is easy, "Oh, you just try some way and maybe people are pissed off and maybe they're not." But probably it's going to be fine and you'll have the chance to try again and iterate and work from it. (00:30:00): But often we get stuck so we don't get to go through those levels of iteration because we want to make sure we're going to get the outcome. We say, "Oh, well, I'm not willing to ever piss anyone off ever. And so I'm just going to be stuck at this step because I haven't figured out what's going to guarantee me." And of course, there's no guarantee. We can never guarantee that people are going to feel a particular way. (00:30:22): So part of asking for what you want effectively is actually bringing some compassion for yourself. Of course, we all want to be sure that the way we ask is going to be effective and no one is going to be mad at us and we're going to get all of our dreams come true. But we don't get that. I wish we did. That would be nice. But is that worth not pursuing your dreams in life?
turns.zh: 即使在那个问题中隐含着一个疑问，对我来说，这就是个问题："哦，我该怎么做才能避免冒犯到任何人？" 这正是阻碍我们前进的根源所在。举个例子，理论上来说，提问很容易——"哦，你可以尝试某种方法，也许人们会生气，也许不会。"但很可能最终没问题，你还有机会再试一次，不断迭代改进。（00:30:00）但我们往往会陷入困境，无法完成这些迭代步骤，因为我们总想确保能得到预期的结果。我们会说："哦，我绝不想冒犯任何人。所以我只能停留在当前阶段，因为我还没找到能保证万无一失的办法。"但显然，世事难料，我们无法保证人们会有特定的反应。（00:30:22）所以，有效地提出自己想要的东西，关键在于对自己怀有同理心。当然，我们都希望自己的提问方式既有效，又不会招人反感，还能让梦想成真。但现实往往事与愿违。真希望能做到完美，但现实毕竟残酷。这值得我们放弃追逐梦想吗？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Such a good point about what you identified and the way... I think a lot of people that think about it, it's just like, "I'd always do this without causing anyone any pain or risking anything going wrong." I think that's, to your point, part of it. So you talk a lot about founders. You work with a lot of founders, a lot of listeners here are not founders, they're product managers, ICs on teams, other functions that don't have "power". Is there anything that you suggest these folks do differently or think about this differently or is it kind of the same thing? In the end everyone has power in some way. How would you think about this if you're just, say, a product manager, individual contributor?
turns.zh: 你提到的观点很深刻。很多思考过这个问题的人都会想：“我总想在不伤害任何人、不冒险出错的情况下做到这一点。” 我认为这正是问题的核心所在。你经常谈到创始人。你和很多创始人合作，但这里很多听众不是创始人，他们是产品经理、团队中的个体贡献者，或者其他没有“权力”的职位。对于这些人，你有什么建议吗？或者说方法是否相似？毕竟每个人都在某种程度上拥有权力。如果你只是个产品经理、个体贡献者，又该如何看待这个问题呢？

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: I think one of the most important balances in terms of the asking step is both asking clearly, but asking with great humility. And this actually works whether you're in a position of power or not because I think a lot of folks will go so far to the end of humility. They say, "Well, I'm not going to say this out loud at all." But in fact, if you're willing to say, I really disagree with this product decision and I would really prefer that we make this different decision. I know it's not my call and I'm just one opinion and a lot of people are going to see things differently and that's fine, but it's important to me that you know that. So what do you think? Are you willing to reconsider this?"
turns.zh: 我认为，在提问环节中，最重要的平衡点在于既要清晰表达，又要保持谦逊。无论你是否处于权力地位，这都适用，因为我发现很多人会走向极端。他们会说："好吧，我根本不会把这事说出来。" 但实际上，如果你愿意说："我真的不赞同这个产品决策，我更希望我们能做出不同的决定。" 我知道这不是我的职责，我只是个人的看法，很多人的看法不同，这没关系，但重要的是让对方知道你的想法。那么你怎么看？你愿意重新考虑一下吗？"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's such a great approach. It's very not scary to say that. It also, I think, highlights something I wanted to touch on is I think people have a lot more influence and power than they think they do. Say a PM on a team disagrees with a plan for a product. People actually care about your opinion and you could actually change things. But just telling them, "I think this is a bad idea." And you often don't. Is that what you find, that people have a lot more influence than they think they do? Anything along those lines that comes up?
turns.zh: 这真是个很棒的方法。说出来一点也不可怕。我觉得这也突显了一个我想提到的观点：人们的影响力和权力远比他们自己想象的要大得多。假设一个团队中的产品经理不同意某个产品计划。人们其实很在意你的意见，你完全可以改变现状。但你往往不愿意这么做。你有没有发现人们的实际影响力比他们自己认为的要大得多？有没有类似的发现？

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: You're giving me deep goosebumps because I think this is a really underappreciated thing in terms of asking for what we want because especially in the PM world, we're trained to look for data. We're not just going to state an opinion. We're going to say, "Oh, the AB test said this. Or 30% of our users do this, or the ROI on this is X." And data is great. We love data for a reason of course. And I think people forget about exactly what you're highlighting, that your relationships matter, and that just your opinion because you believe something or because you want something often that's enough. (00:33:13): Because guess what? You're in a relationship with these people you work with. They care about you. You have some sort of leverage with them. And I think that often people go the other way and say, "Oh, I've got power. I'm going to try and leverage it." But actually, if you go the other direction and you're humble and you say, "I know I can't make you do anything, it's not my call to make. But man, this is really what I want. I'm just going to put it out there and ask." That I think it feels really vulnerable and uncomfortable to not lean on data as a sort of way of saying, "No, no, I'm right, so you should believe what I believe." But just say, "Actually, I don't know that I'm right. This is just what I think and I hope that's enough on its own."
turns.zh: 听你这么说，我真是感触颇深，因为我觉得在争取自己想要的东西这件事上，人们往往忽视了一个非常重要的点——尤其是我们身处项目管理领域的人，被训练得习惯用数据说话。我们不只是陈述观点，而是会说：“哦，A/B测试结果显示了这个结论。或者30%的用户会这样做，投资回报率是X。”数据固然重要——我们对数据的依赖自有其道理。但我觉得人们往往忽略了你强调的这一点：人际关系至关重要。仅仅因为你坚信某件事，或者渴望达成某个目标，光是表达自己的意见往往就足够了。（00:33:13）因为你要知道，你和同事们是建立在信任基础上的关系。他们在乎你，与你存在某种利益交换。我认为很多人会走向另一个极端，试图利用权力优势。但其实，如果你能保持谦逊，坦诚地说：“我知道我无法强制别人做决定，但这确实是我所渴望的。我只是想把想法说出来，然后看看大家是否能接受。”这种真诚的态度远比用数据强硬地说“不，我是对的，所以你们必须认同我的观点”更令人心安。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you find that that's actually a crutch a lot of times to people not saying anything is they don't have that data? They don't have evidence and they just, "I shouldn't say anything. If someone asks for why I don't have a great answer, I just think this is what should be."
turns.zh: 你有没有发现，很多时候人们不表达意见的借口是缺乏数据？他们找不到证据，就说：“我不该说什么。要是有人问为什么我拿不出有力的数据，我只能说‘我只是觉得应该这样’。”

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: Totally. And I think there's a balance there as with anything. Is ignoring data and going in gut all the time, great? Probably not, right? We use data for a reason, but I think there are all these moments when we are making a gut decision and having all the data there means having the opinion set out loud. I think often the dangers of people saying, "Oh, I don't have data to back this up. It's just what I think. And I'm not sure people are going to agree with me, so I'm just not going to say it." (00:34:35): So we don't have the data of all those gut opinions of these subject matter experts in the room, even though that gut information to me is just as important as anything we could get from the SQL database or whatever.
turns.zh: 完全同意。我觉得任何事情都需要平衡。完全无视数据、凭直觉做决定是否明智？恐怕未必。我们用数据是有原因的，但有时直觉判断同样重要。比如，面对专家意见时，即使数据摆在面前，也要大胆说出自己的想法。人们常说：“我没有数据支持这个观点，我只是觉得应该这样，但不确定大家会认同，所以我就不说了。” （00:34:35）所以，我们没有得到房间里所有专家直觉判断的数据，但在我看来，这些直觉信息和从SQL数据库获取的数据同样重要。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Before we move on to step three, you talked about the opposite of asking for what you want. This was just step two is just complaining and being angry later like, "I knew this project was going to fail. I knew this was a terrible deadline. I knew this design was not great." Anything more you want to say along those lines of just like, "If you're not asking for what you want, complaining is often a sign that you should be doing that more"?
turns.zh: 在进入第三步之前，你提到了争取自己想要的东西的反面——抱怨和生气，比如“我就知道这个项目会失败。就知道这个截止日期太紧了。就知道这个设计不行。”你对此有什么想补充的吗？

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: To me, complaints are great inspiration. To me, I love radical candor, for example, where I try to go a step further than radical candor is to not just say, "Hey, here's my feedback. Just wanted you to know." But to say, "And I want something. I would like to see an outcome." And so I think that to me it's all about the effective framing that the complaint is probably not going to be an effective way to do it, but it can be great inspiration to say, "Gosh, that complaining means I'm frustrated. What am I frustrated about? Let me envision that better future. Let me think about what's an effective way to actually move towards that. What's an effective way to communicate that desire that's actually likely to get me towards a yes?" (00:35:58): And so when we actually embrace that sort of frustration, annoying, complaining thing and follow that thread down and think about how to be effective that way, we can actually get something really compelling and useful, but it requires actually embracing that part of ourselves that sometimes we're a little bit ashamed of like, "Oh, I don't like that whiny part of myself. I'm just going to push that one down versus actually taking what it has to say as important data."
turns.zh: 对我来说，抱怨是极好的灵感来源。比如，"激进坦诚"这种方法，我会努力更进一步——不只是说"嘿，这是我的反馈，只是想让你知道。"而是说"我还想得到些什么。我希望看到一个结果。"所以我认为，对我来说，关键在于有效地构建框架。抱怨可能不是有效的解决方式，但它可以成为极好的灵感源泉，让我们思考："天哪，这种抱怨意味着我很沮丧。我为什么会沮丧？让我设想一个更美好的未来。让我思考一种有效的方式来实现这个愿望。一种能真正让我朝着肯定的方向前进的有效沟通方式是什么？"（00:35:58）：当我们真正接纳这种令人沮丧、烦躁、抱怨的心态，顺着这个思路思考如何有效地应对时，我们就能获得真正有价值且实用的见解，但这需要我们接纳自己内心有时会感到些许羞耻的部分，比如"哦，我不喜欢自己这种爱发牢骚的毛病。我只想把它压下去，而不是把它当作重要的信息来认真对待。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a really good point. I think that's actually another blocker for a lot of people is just, "I don't want to be a complaining person. I just want to be like, let's do this. I'm in, let's go. I don't want to be seen as a squeaky wheel." Is there anything you say there about as a resistance point for people?
turns.zh: 这真是个很棒的观点。我认为这对很多人来说也是另一个障碍，他们会想："我不想成为一个爱抱怨的人。我只想说，让我们行动起来。我加入了，出发吧。"你提到这会成为人们的抵触点吗？

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: Well, I'm a big fan of internal family systems, which is this sort of psychotherapy technique that really talks about parts and the sort of parts of ourselves and the ways in which they don't always agree with each other. Part of why I love this approach is, A, because we already use this language. We say, "Part of me thinks this, a part of me thinks that." And really when I talk about how to work through resistance, really it's about embracing and validating all of our parts. (00:37:07): Because often we're really comfortable with one part of ourselves that we think is, "Oh, this part is virtuous and good and great, and this part is whiny and bad, and not great, and I don't respect that part of me as much." So really to sort of ask effectively, we generally need to embrace all these parts and really bring in all the information they're bringing in because if we ignore the part that's really scared to ask, well, then we're going to stay stuck. (00:37:32): Versus if we come in and say, "Hey, buddy, why are you scared? You seem terrified. What's going on? Oh, well man, you think your whole professional reputation has staked on this and you're an imposter and they're going to find out, and then you'll never work again? Well, of course you'd be scared. That makes a ton of sense." And by embracing that, instead of ignoring that and being ashamed of that, that is often how we soften those fears and say, "I know that's scary, but we also know that's not really true. You're not an imposter, right? You're an experienced professional."
turns.zh: 嗯，我非常喜欢内部家庭系统疗法，这是一种心理治疗技术，它真正探讨了我们内心的各个部分，以及这些部分之间有时意见不一致的情况。我喜欢这种方法的部分原因是，A，我们已经在使用这种语言。我们会说："我的一部分认为这样，我的一部分认为那样。"当我谈到如何克服抵触情绪时，关键在于接纳并认可我们所有的部分。（00:37:07）：因为我们通常只对自己某个部分感到自在，认为"哦，这个部分善良、优秀、出色，而那个部分爱发牢骚、不良、不优秀，我不太尊重它的存在。"所以要有效地提问，我们通常需要接纳所有这些部分，并真正吸收它们提供的所有信息。如果我们忽视那个真正害怕提问的部分，那么我们就会停滞不前。（00:37:32）：而如果我们走过去说"嘿，朋友，你为什么这么害怕？你看起来很恐惧。怎么回事？哦，天哪，你觉得整个职业声誉都押在这一件事上，你是个冒牌货，他们会发现的，然后你就再也无法工作了？那你当然会害怕。这完全说得通。"通过接纳这种情绪，而不是忽视和羞耻，我们往往就能化解这些恐惧，并说："我知道这很可怕，但我们也知道这并非事实。你不是冒牌货，对吧？你是一位经验丰富的专业人士。"

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Man, there's so many threads we can't follow here. This whole line of internal family systems, right?
turns.zh: 天哪，这里有太多我们无法深入探讨的思路了。整个内部家庭系统疗法的线索，对吧？

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's its own podcast episode potentially. And then imposter syndrome, we've touched a bunch of different podcast episodes, but I'll avoid going in that direction. Something you reminded me of is we just had Carole Robin on the podcast who taught this class touchy-feely at Stanford for a long time, which is all about helping people learn how to deal with other people, which we never learned in life. It's like a class, how to learn to work with other people.
turns.zh: 这可能得单独做一期播客了。说到冒名顶替综合症，我们在多个播客节目中都谈到过这个话题，但今天我不想深入探讨了。倒是卡罗尔·罗宾（Carole Robin）最近做客我们的播客，她在斯坦福大学长期教授一门名为"触觉感知"的课程，专注于帮助人们学会与他人有效沟通——这正是我们在生活中从未掌握的技能。就好像一堂教人如何与他人合作的课程。

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: I took one of Stanford's T-Group Weekends, summer of 2020, I think a month after George Floyd was murdered and was facilitated by a black woman. And it was one of the most profound transformative weekends of my life. Because T-groups already people rave about them. But having it at that point in history with those people in the room, oof.
turns.zh: 我参加过斯坦福大学2020年夏季的T小组周末活动，那时候乔治·弗洛伊德被谋杀约一个月后，活动由一位黑人女性主持。这是我人生中最具变革性的周末之一。毕竟T小组向来备受赞誉，但在那样的历史背景下，在那个充满特殊氛围的房间里，真是有种震撼人心的力量。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: A lot of tears, I imagine.
turns.zh: 我能想象当时很多人都流下了眼泪。

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: It was crazy. I mean, it was really wild.
turns.zh: 那真是太疯狂了。真的太震撼了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I feel like every single person that has gone through, I think it's called Leaders in Tech is the broader umbrella term. And Carole talked about it. Everyone that has gone through it, 100% have told me that it's a transformative life experience for them. And you had a bonus transformational piece. So anyway, if people want to check out that episode, I will include it in the show notes. But the reason I brought it up is Carole shared this framework for how to actually give feedback in a way where people can receive it that I'll just highlight here. I have it here. (00:39:26): And it's somewhat related to nonviolent communication, which is what you touched on. And she told me, actually, she taught this way before nonviolent communication came out with their whole philosophy. And it's basically when you want to give someone feedback, the template is when you do a behavior, I feel a feeling, and she's big on like say actual feeling word not like, "I feel like, or I feel that," blah, blah, blah. And step three is, "I'm telling you this because..." and then what you want them to change. Do you find that sort of approach helpful?
turns.zh: 我觉得每个参加过"科技领袖"项目（Leaders in Tech）的人，都一致认为这是一次改变人生的深刻体验。卡罗尔还分享了一个如何有效反馈的框架，我现在就把它重点提一下。我手边有相关资料。（00:39:26）：这个框架与非暴力沟通理论有些关联，而你之前也提到了这个理论。卡罗尔说，在非暴力沟通理论诞生之前，她就已经在教授这种理念了。核心步骤是：当你观察到某个行为时，会产生怎样的感受？要注意用具体的感受词汇描述，而不是含糊其辞。第三步是：“我之所以这么说，是因为……”，然后再提出希望对方改进的建议。你觉得这种方法有用吗？

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: I do. I teach the same thing. I think sort of Carole's approach and nonviolent communication, DBT teaches a similar approach. They call dear man.
turns.zh: 我觉得很有用。我的教学内容和卡罗尔的方法，以及非暴力沟通理论、辩证行为疗法（DBT）都有相通之处。DBT有个术语叫“亲切先生”。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: To me, what's DBT?
turns.zh: 对我来说，什么是DBT？

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: It's a dialectical behavioral therapy. It's related to CBT. So there's kind of rough consensus in the sort of personal development world of how to ask. And really what they have in common is around staying really factual because I think that what can we know factually well? We can know our thoughts, we can know our feelings because no one else can know that better than us. Maybe we can trust our eyes. What would a video camera have recorded? And that's about it. (00:40:44): So I think often we get really distracted by all these stories we have about the data, but when we bring it back to that fundamental core of this is what I think, this is what I feel, this is what I've observed in the world, it tends to make the ask a lot clearer versus these stories like you mentioned of, "I feel like you're an asshole." It's like, "Well, that's a story. That's not a fact."
turns.zh: 这是一种辩证行为疗法，与认知行为疗法（CBT）相关。在个人发展领域，人们普遍认同要保持客观事实的核心理念。比如，我们能确切知道自己的想法和感受，因为没有人比我们自己更清楚。或许我们可以相信自己的眼睛——摄像机会记录什么？归根结底，问题往往出在我们被各种数据故事分散注意力上。但当我们回归到核心问题——“这是我的看法”、“这是我的感受”、“这是我在现实中观察到的”时，请求反馈的诉求就清晰多了，而不是像你提到的“我觉得你是个混蛋”这种主观判断。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I feel that is not the right way to say I feel. What do you actually feel? No. Okay, so let's move to step three. We've been going on this whole tangent of therapy and stuff, which is amazing, but let's make sure we cover all three steps. So step one again was articulate what you want. Step two is ask for what you want. What's step three?
turns.zh: 是啊。我觉得这不是表达“我感觉”的正确方式。你到底怎么想的？不行。好的，那我们进入第三步。之前我们一直在讨论心理治疗之类的，这很棒，但我们要确保把三个步骤都讲清楚。第一步是明确自己的需求。第二步是提出自己的要求。第三步是什么？

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: So to me step three is actually the trickiest for most people.
turns.zh: 对我来说，第三步是最难的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So far, they're all tricky to me.
turns.zh: 到目前为止，每一步对我来说都很棘手。

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: Oh yeah, they're all tricky, for sure.
turns.zh: 哦，是的，它们都很难。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: The most tricky.
turns.zh: 最难的。

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: But step three is accept the response. And it might seem so simple, but it actually is kind of subtle. And so one reason is that idea of sort of the whole body yes or the hell yes. Because I think often we really want a yes. And so we're very, very biased to look for a yes versus accepting no, "That was a no." If someone made this face, that's a no. It doesn't matter what comes out of their mouth. And so the challenge of accepting the response is often that of hearing the no, but not over accepting or under accepting it. (00:42:18): Because I think sometimes what people who are really afraid to ask will do is they say, oh, well, that was a no. So it's no forever and I should never ask again. My dream is dead and nothing is ever going to happen for me again." And that's because they get so scared. But actually no, that's over accepting. The no is just from this person right now in the way that you asked, which doesn't necessarily mean anything about the next time you ask to a different person in a different way, in a different time. (00:42:44): And on the flip side, in that sort of more control freak mode, I think for them they'll often skip over the response say, "Well, they said no, but they don't know what they're talking about." Or they're my direct report, so they have to do what I say. So these are all fundamentally disrespectful ways to operate in this relationship. When we're talking about asking for what we want, we're talking about influence. So you need to have good relationships. You can't be influential with a bad relationship. (00:43:13): So really accepting the response is about, yes, I'm going to be genuine about what I want, but I'm also going to genuinely care about you and have deep respect for your ability to consent or not consent to whatever the ask is. Because I think the counterintuitive thing is that often when we really respect people's no's, it can actually be more influential, more motivating. If someone says, "Okay. I'm not ready to deliver this on time." Be like, "Okay. Well, I'm going to give the project to another person." (00:43:46): I'm taking your no at face value. And they say, "Oh gosh, well, I didn't realize that was going to be the consequence. Maybe I can get it done by that time." And so that way you're not forcing them and you're not coercing them, right? You're just saying, "No, you said no? So that your no is no, and I accept that."
turns.zh: 但第三步是接受对方的回应。这听起来很简单，但实际上需要细微的技巧。其中一个原因是那种全身心投入的“是”或者“绝对是”的反应。我觉得我们常常迫切希望得到一个“是”。所以我们非常倾向于寻找“是”的回应，而不是接受“不”的回应。比如如果有人摆出这种表情，那就是“不”。他们说什么并不重要。接受回应的挑战往往在于听到“不”，但又不至于过度接受或过度否定它。（00:42:18）因为我觉得有些害怕开口的人会说，哦，嗯，那就是个“不”。所以这就意味着永远不行，我再也不敢问了。我的梦想破灭了，再也不会有任何事情发生在我身上了。” 这都是因为他们太害怕了。但实际上不行，这就是过度接受。“不”只是这个人当下对你提问的方式的回应，不一定意味着下次你用不同方式、在不同时间、对不同人提问时也会得到同样的回应。（00:42:44）另一方面，以那种更控制狂的模式来看，我认为他们往往会跳过回应，说：“嗯，他们说‘不’，但他们根本不知道自己在说什么。”或者他们是我的直接下属，所以他们必须听我的。这些都是在这种关系中根本不尊重对方的做法。当我们谈论如何提出自己的需求时，我们谈论的是影响力。所以你需要有良好的关系。如果关系不好，怎么可能有影响力呢？（00:43:13）所以真正接受回应就是，是的，我要真诚地表达自己的需求，但我也要真诚地关心你，并深深尊重你是否愿意或不愿意同意我的请求的能力。因为我认为反直觉的是，当我们真正尊重人们的“不”时，它实际上可能更有影响力，更能激发动力。比如有人说：“好吧。我还没准备好按时交付。”你可以说：“好吧。那我把这个项目交给其他人了。” 我完全接受你的“不”。他们会说：“哦，天哪，嗯，我没想到会有这样的后果。也许我能在那之前完成。” 这样你就不会强迫他们，也不会胁迫他们，对吧？你只是说：“不，你说‘不’了？所以你的‘不’就是‘不’，我接受。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So it feels like part of the skill here is preparing, is knowing. Some people just say no and that's okay. That's part of the experience. Part of it is if there's this not yet component... We had Mihika Kapoor on the podcast. She has a PM at Figma and she had this really great approach to building new things within companies is just like everything to her is not yet and no is a not yet. And the way you phrased it is it could just be the way you asked. It could be, maybe they'll agree if you can figure out a better way to pitch the thing. Is there anything more you can add there about just this idea of it's not no forever?
turns.zh: 感觉这里的关键技能之一就是做好准备，了解全局。有些人直接拒绝，那也没关系。这也是一种体验。还有一点是，如果存在尚未确定的因素……我们节目邀请过米希卡·卡普尔。她在Figma担任产品经理，她在公司内部开发新项目时，有一个非常棒的思路——她把一切都视为“尚未确定的状态”，拒绝就是“尚未达成”。你提问的方式可能有问题。如果你能找到更好的方式来阐述项目，客户或许会改变主意。关于“拒绝不等于永久否定”这个观点，你还有什么补充吗？

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: Acceptance of the response is primarily an emotional regulation issue because once we get our emotions intact, it's just, is it yes or is it no? And if it's no, which it probably is, most of the time the world tells us no, then the question is, "All right, what can I learn from this? What am I going to try next?" And so when we're able to emotionally regulate, it's all very cut and dry, right? It's like, "Okay. Here's data to tell me what to try next." (00:45:02): And so really, 99% of the challenge tends to be all the feelings that come up for us when we hear no. Because We hate hearing no. It's so uncomfortable. And so part of the practice of getting good at asking for what we want is recognizing you're going to hear no all the time, and that's completely normal and fine, and it doesn't need to be something so scary or awful.
turns.zh: 接受拒绝主要是一个情绪管理的问题。一旦我们控制住情绪，问题就归结为：“是还是不是？”如果答案是“不是”——而这种情况通常占大多数，世界总会给我们否定——那么关键在于：“好的，我能从中吸取什么教训？接下来我该尝试什么？” 当我们能有效管理情绪时，一切都变得清晰明了：比如，“好的，我需要这些数据来决定下一步该做什么。” （00:45:02） 实际上，99%的挑战都源于听到“不”时产生的情绪。我们讨厌听到“不”，这太令人不适了。因此，学会有效提出需求的关键在于认识到自己会频繁遭遇拒绝，这完全正常且无需恐惧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Easier said than done in real life. Is there an example of either a client of yours... I know you can't actually share specific details, but I'm just curious if there's an example that comes up of someone dealing with this and getting better at it, or your own career.
turns.zh: 在现实中说起来容易做起来难。你能举个客户的例子吗……虽然你不能透露具体细节，但我很好奇是否有客户克服了这种心理，或者你自己在职业生涯中遇到过类似情况。

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: I gave a talk about this sort of right after it happened, but I was fired from Slack three different times, which I feel like has to be some kind of startup record. I don't know who would be the record-keeping body for this. But now 10 years on, I have different perspective, of course. And so this was almost exactly 10 years ago, spring of 2014 and I just gotten the job as the first PM at Slack. It was already the hottest thing out there. It was only a couple dozen employees. (00:46:03): I came in excited, but also a little insecure because I had just come off my breakup with my co-founder. I just wanted to put my head down and do a good job. I was engaged at the time, so Slack already knew I was going to be going away on a bachelor or backpacking trip. I have a wedding and honeymoon in the fall. And so I came in naive and overconfident of, "I've been a founder. I've worked on iconic products. I know how to do this. I'm a pro. I'm just going to go in and do the work." (00:46:32): So instead of getting really clear on what does success look like here or what's your culture or what are your expectations of me, I just went in and made my best guess and went for it. And lo and behold, turns out what I came in with, that supreme overconfidence was not what they wanted at all. They'd kind of been in the trenches reinventing from the game to Slack. They'd been through layoffs, really hard times together. So they wanted someone to come in humble and to earn their trust of this kind of core team that had been together for years. (00:47:07): I just didn't get any of that. I wasn't hearing that feedback. I wasn't hearing those nos, and I wasn't articulating what I wanted. What I wanted was really very basic. I just wanted to figure out how to do a good job, and I wanted to have a good relationship with the CEO because I was working for him. And you need to have a good relationship with your boss. But the problem was in the first firing anyway was I had not articulated those goals. (00:47:36): And so I shouldn't have been surprised when six weeks into my tenure at Slack, I came back from my backpacking trip with my bachelor buddies, and I had an email in my inbox saying, "Hey, you're fired. It seems like it's not working out. Let me know how you want to wrap it up." So as you can imagine, I freaked out. I loved this job, I love this company, so I profusely apologized. I said, "I'll do whatever it takes. I'm so sorry. I'm going to be committed to turn this around." (00:48:07): And so early stage startup turns out firing doesn't always stick. Monday morning, I had my job back. But obviously things were not the same as they'd been before because in the second era, what I wanted was sort of better articulated more clear, but all of a sudden that fear that had been under the surface, that insecurity was now very, very present every day because I was terrified of was I going to get fired? Was I going to not make the most of this opportunity? And so I went fully into people pleaser mode. And so that meant that even though what I desperately wanted was to have this good relationship was to be successful, build a great product. I had a year of one-on-ones with the CEO. (00:48:52): I never, never ever asked for what I wanted. I never said it out loud because I was scared. I was scared of what the consequences were. I knew there were a hundred PMs standing behind me ready to take my job if the CEO is ever a moment unhappy with me. I said, "No, I'm not going to take the risk. I'm too scared of what the consequences might be." And so I held all that fear and all those desires of, "I just want to do a great job. I want us to be awesome partners and build this amazing industry changing product." (00:49:22): I never said any of that stuff out loud. I just put my head down and I tried to obey. And so as you can imagine, this didn't work very well. I was feeling horrible day to day. I was terrified of this guy I was working for. And so again, I shouldn't have been surprised, but I was, when I got fired for the second time. It wasn't quite firing. But this time I'd come back from my honeymoon and I had a phone call on Monday that said, "Seems like product management is not working out for Slack. We're actually just going to get rid of product. You're going to be user research. It's going to be fine." (00:49:56): And for me, I love user research, but that was the beginning of my career. I was not interested in going back to that. What was fascinating was at that point, I was actually able to articulate what I wanted there and was willing to say it out loud. Because what I wanted was, "No, let's keep me in product. I've got an idea for how we can run it." So I wrote a proposal, I sent it around to the management team. Turns out, when you actually ask for what you want out loud, you're much more likely to get it. (00:50:21): And so within a week, this new plan had traction with the management team team and I had my old job back again. Everything was fine except of course it wasn't fine because now I was scared, but the stakes seemed really high, and this is where that deep imposter syndrome sit in. I was like, "Am I even any good at this? Should I even be in product management? Am I ever going to work in this industry again? Is this going to be my dark secret that I take to the grave that Stewart Butterfield fired me three times?" (00:50:58): I think what I couldn't be with in that moment was the no's, because I was getting no after no after no after no from Stewart and the rest of the management team saying, "What you're doing is not working for us, right? Your ask are not landing. You're not being effective in the way that you want to be effective." And because I wasn't able to hear those no's again, because to that emotional regulation standpoint, I couldn't handle the feelings of like, "Ugh, maybe what I'm doing is not good enough." (00:51:26): So instead of pointing the finger at myself, I pointed the finger at him. I said, "You know what? Actually this guy, he's not such a great manager. He's not so good at product. I'm the one who was on the ground with the users. I know what's right." Against all evidence to the contrary, by the way, is this product luminary, visionary, famous person. (00:51:45): So clearly not based on any facts, but it was an emotional issue of I couldn't deal with the reality of what I was doing was not working. And so again, because I was not articulating what I wanted, I was not asking for it and I certainly was not listening to the no's. I shouldn't have been surprised when finally the third time it came down, and this time it was serious because we had HR. (00:52:09): So it turns out once you hire HR, the firings are final. And so I only made it to a year at Slack and it was a year of just utter torture because I spent that year being fully out of integrity with myself. Never saying what I really wanted, how I really felt because it didn't feel safe. I was too scared. I kept it all inside. And it took me six months or a year even after that to really feel safe and okay again. It was a serious decompression time. (00:52:39): My wife and I had a baby during that time. I was on zero sleep. It was a rough, rough period. But the irony is that when I actually came out of that experience, the reality of it was extremely simple. I hadn't articulated what I wanted. I hadn't asked for what I wanted. I had not listened to the no's in response to my non-ask. (00:53:02): And so of course I was unhappy with the result. Why would I have expected anything different? I wasn't the victim. Stewart wasn't the villain. It was just ineffective asking. And so to me, especially because I was already on that path towards coaching, that lesson hit really hard in terms of how do we make this work more sustainable? (00:53:24): We stay in integrity with ourselves even when it's hard, even when it's scary, even when we don't know exactly what the outcome is going to be. And so that's really the story of how I became a coach, of seeing exactly how much I'd screwed up at Slack and seeing how much I had suffered and how much a lot of people suffer in these similar circumstances. All you have to do to turn it around is ask for what you want. (00:53:45): So this is why I'm so passionate about this stuff because it can sound so fluffy to say, "Oh, focus on integrity. Honor your desires. No, it's real life stuff of a year of suffering, of pain, of fear." I don't want other people to be going through that and that's why I'm so passionate about this stuff.
turns.zh:
事情发生后不久，我就去做了相关分享，但我被Slack解雇了三次，我觉得这肯定创下了初创公司解雇员工的纪录。不知道谁会负责记录这类数据。不过十年后的现在，我当然有了不同的看法。2014年春天，我刚加入Slack担任首位产品经理时，它已经是当时最热门的公司之一，当时只有几十名员工。（00:46:03）我满怀激动地加入，但也略带不安，因为刚与联合创始人分手。我只想埋头工作，做好本职工作。当时我已订婚，所以Slack早知道我会去度单身派对或背包旅行，还要参加秋季的婚礼和蜜月。于是我天真又自信地加入，觉得自己曾是创始人，参与过标志性产品，知道如何胜任这份工作。但（00:46:32）我没有仔细了解公司的成功标准、文化理念或对我的期望，只是凭直觉行事，结果发现这种自负完全不符合他们的要求。他们从游戏领域转型至Slack，经历过裁员，共同度过艰难时光，渴望新人能谦逊入职，赢得核心团队的信任。（00:47:07）但我完全没领会这些信息，听不到反馈，无法清晰表达需求。我的诉求其实很简单：做好工作，与CEO建立良好关系，毕竟是为他工作。然而第一次被解雇的原因就是我未能明确这些目标。（00:47:36）六周后，我从单身派对归来，收到了解雇邮件：“你不适合这份工作，请处理离职事宜。”我顿时慌了，热爱这份工作和公司，赶紧道歉：“我会全力以赴，弥补过失。” 但初创公司解雇员工并不意味着终结。周一早上我就复职了。但一切已然不同。第二阶段，我更清晰地表达了需求，却突然被深藏的恐惧、缺乏安全感吞噬，时刻担心被解雇或错失机会。于是我陷入讨好型人格，明明渴望成功却不敢表达。（00:48:07）一年间，我与CEO每周单独沟通，却从未主动争取真正想要的东西，害怕得罪别人。即便知道有百名PM候补，CEO稍有不满随时可能接手，我仍说："不，我不冒险了。"
所有那些想法，比如“我只想把工作做好。我想和团队成为出色的合作伙伴，一起打造这个改变行业的惊人产品。”（00:49:22）：我从未大声说出过这些话。我只是埋头苦干，努力服从指令。可想而知，这样下去效果并不理想。我每天都情绪低落，害怕为我工作的那个老板。结果可想而知，当我第二次被解雇时，虽然严格来说不算正式裁员，但我度蜜月回来后，周一接到电话：“产品管理部门在Slack这里似乎不太行。我们决定裁掉整个产品团队。你去负责用户研究吧，一切都会好起来的。” （00:49:56）对我来说，用户研究是热爱的事业，但那只是我职业生涯的起点。我没兴趣回归那个岗位。有趣的是，那时我第一次勇敢地表达自己的诉求：“不，别裁掉我！我有办法让产品部门运作起来。”于是我写了份提案，发给管理层。结果发现，当你大声说出自己的需求时，成功的概率会大得多。 （00:50:21）一周内，新方案就得到了管理层的认可，我重获旧职。表面上一切顺利，但暗流涌动。深层的冒名顶替综合症让我焦虑不安：“我真的行吗？我该留在产品管理吗？还能在这一行立足吗？斯图尔特·巴特菲尔德三次解雇我，这会成为我永远无法释怀的秘密吗？” （00:50:58）最让我难以承受的是一次次的否定——斯图尔特和管理层不断否定我的工作：“你不符合我们的要求！你的方案没用！你根本不专业！” 而我无法再承受这些否定，因为从情绪调节的角度看，我无法面对“或许我真的不够好”的现实。 （00:51:26）于是我把矛头转向他人：“这家伙根本不是好经理！他不擅产品！我才是和用户打交道的人！我才是对的！” 尽管这与事实相去甚远，但当时我情绪失控，无法面对自己工作的失败。第三次裁员时，HR介入，情况变得严峻。 （00:52:09）事实证明，一旦引入HR，裁员就是板上钉钉的事了。我在Slack只待了一年，整年如同身处炼狱——因为我从未真实表达过自己的需求，无法直面内心，活在恐惧中，把一切都藏在心底。甚至六个月后我才慢慢恢复正常，经历了一段严重的心理疏导期。 （00:52:39）那一年，我们迎来了宝宝的降生。
时间。我当时睡眠严重不足。那是一段极其艰难的时期。但讽刺的是，当我真正走出那段经历时，现实变得异常简单。我没有清晰表达自己的需求，没有主动争取想要的东西，也没有倾听他人对我的请求的拒绝。（00:53:02）所以当然我对结果不满意。我又怎么能期待别样的结果呢？我不是受害者。斯图尔特也不是反派。只是因为请求方式失效了。对我来说，尤其因为我当时已经走上了教练之路，这个教训让我深刻反思：如何让这种模式更可持续？（00:53:24）即使在困难时期、面对恐惧时、甚至当我们不确定结果如何时，我们也要坚守自我。这就是我成为教练的历程——我清醒地意识到自己在Slack时的诸多失误，目睹了自己承受的痛苦，也见证了许多人在类似处境下深受折磨。只要勇敢地提出自己的需求，一切都能迎刃而解。（00:53:45）这就是我为何如此热衷于分享这些理念的原因。说起来可能显得冠冕堂皇——"专注于诚信，尊重自己的愿望"。但这背后是整整一年的煎熬、痛苦和恐惧。我不希望其他人经历同样的困境，这就是我对此充满热情的原因。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow, what a story. I love that it's kind of a microcosm of everything we've talked about. You've did all the things that you teach people to avoid.
turns.zh: 哇，真是个精彩的故事。我觉得它恰好是我们所讨论的所有问题的缩影。你把人们应该避免做的事全做了一遍。

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: Exactly.
turns.zh: 太对了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And I think what's interesting is you went through these three phases. Interestingly, at the beginning, your first phase was you were not hearing the no's, but it was rooted in this confidence that you're a founder, you're awesome. They're so lucky to have you. I know what I'm doing, get out of my way. And then the third phase, you also, the issue there was you weren't hearing the no's, but it was more from fear of being fired again. And so it's interesting that there's these different reasons you're not hearing what people are actually saying.
turns.zh: 我觉得有趣的是，你经历了三个阶段。很有意思的是，一开始，你的第一阶段是听不进别人的否定，但根源在于你作为创始人的自信，觉得自己很棒，他们能拥有你真是幸运。我知道自己在做什么，别挡我的路。而第三阶段，你同样没听进别人的否定，但更多是出于害怕再次被解雇。所以很有趣的是，你没听进别人真正想说的话的原因各不相同。

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: Totally. Well, and to me, the first one is about articulation as well because I think that if in the beginning it articulated that, "Yeah, I'm confident, but actually I want to do a really good job and I want to have good relationships. So let me think about intentionally, how do I create those outcomes?" But because I hadn't articulated that's what I wanted, it didn't even occur to me like, "Oh yeah, I need to do some intentional relationship building, figure out some metrics for success." (00:55:11): It was an early stage startup. There wasn't a ton of sort of process or structure in place, suffice to say. And so if I wanted that, I needed to create it myself, but because I hadn't articulated that any of that was important to me, I just flew by the seat of my pants and it took failing to get some data to say, "Ooh, yeah, maybe I need to look at this more closely."
turns.zh: 完全同意。对我来说，第一个阶段还关乎清晰表达自己的意图。我觉得如果一开始你能明确表达：“是的，我很自信，但实际上我想把工作做好，也想和大家建立良好的关系。所以让我有意识地思考，如何达成这些目标？”但因为我没有明确表达这是我想要的，我就根本没有意识到，“哦，对啊，我需要有意识地建立关系，制定成功的衡量标准。”（00:55:11）那是个早期初创公司。可以说，当时没有太多流程或结构。所以如果我想要这些，就得自己去创造，但因为我没有明确这些对我很重要，我就只能随机应变。直到失败后，我才获得了一些数据，说：“哦，对啊，也许我需要更仔细地考虑一下这个问题。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I imagine you've gone through this exercise many times, but say you were to do it again, what would you do differently and what do you think would've happened? Do you think you would've stayed there for many, many years, had a product at Slack at this point? Just imagining that reality, what would you have done differently? And then what would you have imagined have turned out?
turns.zh: 我想你肯定多次经历过这种情况，但假设你现在再做一次，你会做些不同的事吗？你觉得结果会怎样？你觉得自己会不会在那里待很多年，现在已经在Slack做产品了？想象一下那种情况，你会做些不同的事吗？然后你又会预想得到什么样的结果？

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: Well, I mean obviously broadly, I would've asked for what I wanted and what I wanted was I wanted to do the best work of our life. I wanted to have a deep professional partner in the CEO and the rest of the product and management team. And I wanted to produce great work that people loved. And that was part of why I was attracted to the culture and the mission and the company. And so this is what's tricky is of course, that's what I would've done. Now, do I know what the outcome would've been? (00:56:16): No, I might've been fired even sooner. They might've said, "No, this is not working out. Let's just be done here." So that's what's tricky about this is it really isn't about the outcome. Of course, asking for what you want makes you more likely to get the outcome you want, but you don't do it for guarantee of a certain outcome because no one can promise you that. You do it so you can stay in integrity with yourself and not suffer through all this. Because at least then I would've said, "You know what? It didn't work out. At least I'm not sitting here suffering. I can get another job at another startup. It's not the end of the world." (00:56:51): And I think that the mistake we make is pretending that it is of saying, going into fight or flight and saying, "This is a severe existential threat to who I am and my safety in the world," versus being like, "I'm disappointed. I wish it had worked out, but it didn't."
turns.zh: 嗯，我是说显然从大方向上讲，我本该去争取自己想要的东西，而我想要的是做出一生中最出色的工作。我希望能与首席执行官以及产品和管理团队的其他成员建立深厚的职业伙伴关系。我还想创作出人们喜爱的优秀作品。这也是我被这家公司的文化、使命和团队吸引的原因之一。所以关键在于，尽管我本可以做到这些，但我不知道最终结果会怎样。（00:56:16）：不，我很可能更早被解雇。他们可能会说：“不行，这样下去不行，还是算了吧。”所以这里的难点不在于结果。当然，勇于争取自己想要的东西会让你更有可能得到理想的结果，但你这么做并非为了保证必然成功——毕竟没人能给你这样的保证。你这么做是为了保持自我忠诚，不必为此深陷痛苦之中。因为至少那样的话，我还能说：“嗯，事情没成。但至少我现在不用在这里煎熬了。我可以去另一家初创公司试试。天塌不下来。”（00:56:51）：我认为我们常犯的错误是假装这是一场生死攸关的斗争，说：“这对我的人格和安全构成了严重威胁。”而实际上应该说：“我很失望，我希望事情能成，但没能成。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a really profound point that this practice isn't necessarily to just have everything work out beautifully and to get the things you're looking for. It's to feel like you did, which you could have and to feel integrity with yourself that you did what you needed to do and you're not going to regret something down the road.
turns.zh: 这真是一个深刻的观点——这种做法不一定是为了让一切都完美无缺，得到你想要的东西。而是为了感受到自己本可以做到本可以拥有，保持自我忠诚，知道自己尽力了，未来也不会追悔莫及。

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: Indeed.
turns.zh: 确实。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I'm going to take a quick tangent down the being the first PM route real quick. There's a lot of people that think about being the first PM at a startup join as the first PM. I imagine you work with people asking for advice along these lines. It's classically a very challenging role. Many people don't last. Many people follow your trajectory where it's like, "Oh, shit. What have I done?" Any advice for people that are a first PM at a company or startup or thinking about that role?" What can you tell them to help them be successful or at least not suffer?
turns.zh: 我要快速聊聊初任产品经理的经历。很多初创公司的人都想成为首任产品经理。我想你肯定会遇到很多人咨询这方面的问题。这通常是个极具挑战的角色，很多人做不下去，很多人会走你的老路——“天哪，我这是干了什么啊？”对于初任产品经理，或者正考虑这个角色的人，你有什么建议吗？能给他们些什么帮助，让他们更容易成功，或者至少不那么痛苦？

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: To me, it really is about the relationship with the CEO or with the founders because that's the root of a lot of the issues that come out of that scenario because it's not always you. In my story, I think it was primarily about me, but I also work with a lot of founders who are going through really tough things. My clue to people who report to a founder is to say, "Imagine if you're confused about how your founder is behaving. Imagine that they're terrified all the time, and see if that makes their behavior more clear." (00:58:38): Because it is scary to be a founder. Everything is on your shoulders. And I think a lot of people do feel that sense of high stakes all the time. And so I think being real about that of what is the state that the person or the people you're working for are in and sort of working within that versus sort of pretending that it's something else or wishing that it were something else is the path to having a healthy relationship. Because if you don't have a healthy relationship with the person you're working for, you're not going to get anything done. You're not going to succeed in any meaningful way.
turns.zh: 对我而言，关键在于与CEO或创始人的关系，因为这正是许多问题产生的根源——毕竟问题往往不只出在你个人身上。在我的经历中，我认为主要问题出在我身上，但我也与许多正经历巨大挑战的创始人合作过。给向创始人汇报的人的建议是：“想象如果你对创始人的行为感到困惑。想象他们时刻处于恐惧之中，看看这是否能让他们的行为更清晰。”（00:58:38）：因为成为创始人确实令人心生恐惧。一切都压在你的肩上。我认为很多人确实时刻感受到高风险感。因此，坦然面对你所服务的人的真实处境，并在此基础上开展工作——而不是假装别的情况或期待理想中的状态——才是建立健康关系的关键。毕竟，如果与你共事的人关系不融洽，你什么事也做不成，任何有意义的成功都无从谈起。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that framework of how to think about why a founder is behaving in a certain way. Just maybe a last following thread there is just what should people look for to help them understand if the founder and them are a good fit, if they're going to have a good time working with that founder? Is there anything just like questions they might ask or ways of operating that are useful to understand like, "Okay, I think I'll be okay with this founder in this company as the first PM or not.
turns.zh: 我很欣赏这种思考创始人行为动因的框架。最后再追问一句：人们该如何判断自己与创始人是否合拍，能否愉快共事？有没有什么问题可以用来判断？比如：“好吧，我觉得我能适应这家公司的创始人，担任首任产品经理。”

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: I think it's a hard thing to generalize about, but to me it really is about understanding expectations. I guess this is a predictable coming from me, "But what do you really want? Because I think that often the founders put together a job description, but then they're faced with a real human being who has real human subtleties and things they're good at or not so good at." And so being very, very clear about expectations and of figuring out collaboratively a way to work together that's effective to me is there's no guarantees of course, but it gives you a more sure path to having a productive relationship. (01:00:13): It's actually something that I recommend to a lot of founders for maybe their first 10 or 15, or 20 employees of just have a relationship design conversation with each of them when they're first hired. Because I think a lot of us come in naive the way I did, assuming, "Oh yeah, I'm just going to come in and do my thing the way I've always done it. It's going to be fine." Versus coming in and saying, "I actually don't know how I'm going to operate at this company. I have range like anyone has range, and I don't know what this company needs and who else is here and sort of what my role and what my place is going to be within these other people. And so by really understanding that intentionally and not from a place of performance management, you're already doing this poorly, you're in big trouble. But what is the best way to work together given who we have now and what we want and what we need? Let's figure it out.
turns.zh: 我认为这很难一概而论，但对我而言，关键在于理解对方的期望。我猜这听起来很老生常谈，但我还是要说：但你真正想要的是什么？因为我发现很多创始人会制定一份职位描述，但面对一个真实的人——这个人有自己的细微差别，有擅长和不擅长之处——时往往手足无措。因此，尽早明确期望，并共同探索高效合作之道——我知道这没有万无一失的保证，但至少能为建立富有成效的关系指明方向。（01:00:13）：这也是我给许多创始人的建议：在他们招聘的前10、15或20名员工时，就与每人进行一次关系设计对话。因为我们很多人都曾像我一样天真，心想：“哦，我只要来做自己，按老习惯行事就没问题了。” 而不是坦然承认：“我其实不知道如何在公司里开展工作。每个人都有局限性，我不了解公司的需求，不清楚其他成员是谁，也不清楚自己在团队中的角色和定位。” 因此，主动去理解这些问题——而不是从绩效管理的角度出发——你已经把事情搞砸了。但基于现有的人员、需求和目标，如何才能高效合作？让我们一起探索吧。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Coming back to our core topic, is there anything that we didn't cover, anything that I should have asked you about the skill, the art of asking for what you want? Anything else you want to leave listeners with?
turns.zh: 回到我们的核心话题，有没有我们没涉及的方面？有没有我应该问你但遗漏的关于“如何勇敢争取自己想要的”的技巧或艺术？还有什么想留给听众的启示？

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: I do want to mention something that I hear a lot from founders when I talk about the piece of working through resistance because I think a lot of them say, "Oh, you want me to let go of fear and focus on what I want? Well, I mean, I've been running from fear my whole career. That's how I'm so hard-working and I'm so smart is I'm always afraid I'm not good enough." (01:01:34): Am I going to be able to do this job without fear hounding me every step of the way? I just remember the first time I heard this, it broke my heart, and now I've heard it dozens of times I'd say. So I mean, it really is. I think it's a belief that sits deep in the hearts of a lot of us high achieving Silicon Valley tech types of, "My fear of not being good enough is what drives me to be great." (01:02:00): And I just want to come out here and say there's other ways to motivate. You can motivate based on joy, based on vision, based on your inspiration in this vision of what you want. I think a lot of folks I talk to are skeptical understandably because operated a different way their whole life and all I can really say is try it. Try following an inspiring vision that's really meaningful to you and just see what it's like to not be living in fear all the time because it is a big difference and it's really meaningful. It matters a lot.
turns.zh: 我确实想提一下我在和创始人谈论克服阻力时经常听到的一个观点，因为我发现很多创始人会说：“哦，你想让我放下恐惧，专注于自己想要的东西？可是，我整个职业生涯都在逃避恐惧啊。正是因为总担心自己不够好，我才如此努力，如此聪明。”（01:01:34）：我能在没有恐惧感的驱使下完成这份工作吗？我记得第一次听到这种说法时，它让我心碎，而现在我已经听过几十次了。所以我要说，这确实是一种根深蒂固的信念，深深扎根于许多硅谷高成就者的内心——“对自己不够好的恐惧，正是推动我走向卓越的动力。”（01:02:00）：我想在这里强调，还有其他激励方式。你可以基于快乐、愿景、灵感来激励自己，追随对你有意义的愿景。我发现很多和我交谈过的人都心存疑虑，这很正常，因为他们一生都习惯了另一种处事方式。我能说的，就是去尝试吧。尝试追随一个对你真正有意义的鼓舞人心的愿景，看看不一直活在恐惧中是什么感觉，因为这真的会带来巨大的改变，意义非凡。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So is the fear there that if they ask for what they want, they'll get what they want and they let go of this drive to prove themselves? And is that the fear? How is it that they move away from that need to prove themselves?
turns.zh: 那么，恐惧的根源是否在于，如果他们去争取自己想要的，就会得到想要的东西，于是他们就放下了这种证明自己的驱动力？这就是恐惧的本质吗？他们是如何摆脱这种需要证明自己的需求的？

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: Well, I mean that's a longer story. I would say managing our own fear as a sort of lifelong practice. I'm not going to claim I'm anywhere near done with it. But I guess I'd just say that I think part of the big shift I see in personal development for people I work with is from saying, "Oh, no, my fear is good. I need it. It's keeping me safe." (01:03:16): To saying, "Fear is for when there's a tiger chasing you and there's no tiger chasing me." I'm sitting in my office in a desk chair on a zoom call. There's no real danger here. And so fear is not particularly functional. And so when they start realizing that, the practice becomes, "Oh yeah, I'm feeling afraid." But I'm reminding myself there's not a tiger in the room. If I really want to get things done, achieve my goals, I need to focus on vision on what I want to achieve in the world, not on avoiding all these fears. So that's the short of it.
turns.zh: 嗯，这说来话长。我会说管理我们自己的恐惧是一种终身修行。我不敢说自己已经完全掌握了这门技艺。但我觉得我所看到的我合作对象在个人发展方面的重大转变，是从说“哦，不，我的恐惧是有益的，我需要它，它能保护我。”（01:03:16），到说“恐惧是在老虎追着你跑时产生的，而现在没有老虎追着我跑。”我坐在办公室的椅子上，参加视频会议。这里没有真正的危险。所以恐惧在这里并无实际作用。当他们开始意识到这一点时，修行就变成了“哦，是的，我感到害怕。”但我提醒自己，房间里没有老虎。如果我真的想把事情做好，实现我的目标，我就需要专注于愿景，专注于我想在世界上实现的目标，而不是逃避所有这些恐惧。这就是要点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. It reminds me, we have a chat... I had a chat with Matt Mochari, and we spent a bunch of time on dealing with fear and overcoming fear. So folks want to dig deeper there. They could check out that episode. Just maybe one more question before we get to our very exciting lightning round. I want to take us to Contrarian Corner, classic contrarian corner. I'm curious if there's anything that you have a contrarian opinion about, something that you believe that most other people don't.
turns.zh: 太棒了。这让我想起，我们和马特·莫查里（Matt Mochari）进行过一次对话，花了很多时间讨论如何应对恐惧和克服恐惧。所以如果有人想深入探讨，可以去看看那期节目。在我们即将进入令人兴奋的闪电问答环节之前，我想带大家进入“逆向思维角”，这个经典的逆向思维环节。我很好奇，你是否有任何与大多数人不同的逆向观点？

turns.speaker: Kenneth Berger
turns.en: For me, I'm not a big believer in discipline that I think some folks come to coaching looking for a drill sergeant and say, "All right. Shout at me and tell me to do better." And I start to say, "That's not how I operate." Because it's not the discipline doesn't work, but it's like people-pleasing. It's a short-term coping strategy. Discipline will get you in the gym for a week, but it's not going to get you in the gym for a year. The people who are in the gym for a year are doing it because they want to. (01:04:49): There's actually something that's motivating for them in that. It's not just, "Oh, I hate this, but I'm going to go anyway." And so I try to be really clear with people about that, that I'm not going to be the drill sergeant because it's unsustainable. Someone shouting at you is not going to get you moving towards what you want in life over multiple years. It's days or weeks or even hours thing. And so I really look for a higher bar to say, "Let's look for true long-term sustainable motivation," which means relying on vision, pursuing what you want.
turns.zh: 对我而言，我不太相信那种纪律性训练。我觉得有些人来找教练时，希望对方像个严厉的教官一样大喊：“好吧，对我大吼大叫，告诉我要做得更好。”但我会说：“这不是我的行事方式。”因为纪律性训练并不可靠，它只是一种讨好他人的短期应对策略。纪律性训练能让你坚持锻炼一周，但无法让你坚持一年。那些坚持锻炼一年的人，是因为他们真心想这么做。（01:04:49）：其实真正激励他们的是内心的驱动力。不只是“我讨厌这个，但还是会去”。所以我会跟人们坦白，我不会当那种严厉的教官，因为那不可持续。别人对你大吼大叫，无法让你在多年里朝着自己的人生目标前进。这只是短暂的激励，持续不了多久。因此，我更倾向于寻求更高层次的动力，比如明确愿景、追寻梦想。

And he builds this playground for children, and that's actually his legacy. Sorry, actually, spoiler alert. Whoops, should've.

turns.en: They're going to get a bunch of traffic. They're like, "What the hell just happened?" Teafromtaiwan.com amazing. Do you have a favorite life motto that you often come back to, find useful, share with friends or family and work around life?
